metadata.title: Claude, Configured
metadata.subtitle: Installing and Customizing Plugins
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: does installing a plugin already make it fit your business? Explain the machinery — install is trivial, the customize conversation is where the actual fit happens — and judge the design choices that put it together that way.
metadata.anchor_pair: NB08 -> NB11 (the marketing studio Q&A, paid off with the tuned output diverging from generic)
metadata.one_flag: N/A - direct mechanism description throughout (see SCRIPT.md One-flag audit)

beats.narration_text: Here's the mistake — thinking installing is the customization. The install is just the download. A plugin arrives with generic defaults tuned for nobody in particular. So how do you actually make it customized, for your business?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'How do I install a plugin for my business?', hesitates on 'install', corrects to 'customize', lands the real question

props.text:
How do I
install a plugin
for my business?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('install' -> 'customize') lands on screen.

beats.narration_text: Open the plugin section and you get a library — an official set plus community additions. Each listing tells you what it does and what it covers. The design here is a marketplace, not a catalogue: you browse by function, not by name, so you find a plugin by the problem you're trying to solve.

Click install and it downloads, activates, ready — no setup wizard. Here's what's actually happening: the plugin registers itself with the app. Skills switch on when they're contextually relevant, slash commands appear in your menu, connectors sit waiting to be authorized. Zero configuration first — the trade-off is that you get generic behavior until you customize it.

production_viz.label: CLICK. THEN IT'S THERE.
production_viz.caption: skills, commands, and connectors just appear

beats.narration_text: A colleague shares one, or you pull it from the community — it arrives as a file. Click upload, pick the file, and it installs the same way as anything from the official library. The design choice here matters: side-loaded plugins get the same install path as first-party ones. Same couple of minutes, same integration surface.

Out of the box, a plugin runs on sensible defaults — generic best practice for its domain. Useful, and honest about it. But you don't do generic work. You have your own process, your own vocabulary, your own way in. What you got from the install is a starting point, not a fit.

production_viz.label: YOU DON'T DO GENERIC
production_viz.caption: useful — but not built for you yet

beats.narration_text: Click customize and here's the design choice: it doesn't open a settings panel. It starts a conversation. It asks about your workflow, your preferences, your tools; you answer in plain language; the plugin adjusts from what you said. They chose language over checkboxes because the details that matter can't be enumerated in advance — they have to be described.

The mechanism is a loop, always the same shape: it asks, you answer, it calibrates. Ask again, answer again, it tightens. Two questions or twenty — the loop scales with how much detail you're willing to give it.

production_viz.label: ASK, ANSWER, CALIBRATE
production_viz.caption: the same loop, two questions or twenty

beats.narration_text: Depth is your call. Run the defaults — fine, still useful, if generic. Or spend a few minutes and it starts to feel built for your business. This scales with how central the domain is to your day: don't tune what you barely use; tune deeply what you touch every hour.

production_viz.label: YOUR CALL, YOUR DEPTH
production_viz.caption: scales with how central this is to your day

beats.narration_text: Say you install a marketing plugin and click customize. First question — what does your business do, and who are your customers? You answer: a small web design studio, clients are professional-services firms with no marketing team of their own. That's the anchor. Watch what it gets used for.

This is the studio the plugin is about to learn — one person, a few screens, real clients. And these are the clients it now understands: accountants, lawyers, financial advisors who need a modern site but have no marketing operation of their own. Not a persona document, not a hypothetical audience — the actual shape of your business.

production_viz.label: THE STUDIO, AND ITS CLIENTS
production_viz.caption: not a hypothetical persona — your business

beats.narration_text: A few more answers — voice is professional but approachable, no jargon; formats are social posts and a monthly newsletter. The plugin locks all of it in: audience, voice, formats. These aren't preferences it consults later; they become the frame every future output is generated inside.

production_viz.label: VOICE, AUDIENCE, FORMATS
production_viz.caption: locked in from your own answers

beats.narration_text: Now the output changes. Ask for a content calendar and you get posts and newsletter topics — not viral video scripts, not press releases. A competitive scan targets other web studios, not enterprise agencies. Same request, different answer — because the plugin isn't reasoning from generic marketing best practice any more; it's reasoning from the studio you just described.

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — TUNED
production_viz.caption: the same request, a different answer

beats.narration_text: Some plugins are self-contained — useful out of the box, wired to nothing. Others get dramatically more useful the second you connect them to the tools you already run. This is a design decision each plugin author made, not a universal rule: know which kind you installed before you decide how far to go.

A sales plugin researches a prospect from public info alone — decent. Connect it to your CRM and it pulls in your relationship history and every past conversation. Same shape for data plugins: give them files, or connect the live database and they work on your actual numbers, no exporting. The trade-off is authorization surface — you're granting real access — for a genuine step up in usefulness.

Connecting is the standard login flow — you authorize access the same way you'd link any other app to any other app. And here's what matters about the design: it's optional. Start without connections, add them later once you can see what value they'd add. They chose progressive commitment over up-front setup.

production_viz.label: AUTHORIZE, THEN REACH
production_viz.caption: the same flow as any third-party app

beats.narration_text: Want a smaller workspace? Disable a plugin without removing it. The customization stays preserved, waiting — flip it back on and it's exactly as you left it. Nothing you taught it is lost. Disable is not uninstall; the two operations are separated on purpose.

production_viz.label: OFF WITHOUT ERASING
production_viz.caption: nothing you taught it is lost

beats.narration_text: Plugins keep improving — features get added, issues get fixed, updates handled for you. The design choice worth naming: you don't have to manage versions. Worth checking in occasionally to see what's new that you might actually use, because the plugin you tuned last month may quietly have grown a capability worth another five minutes of your time.

Loading up on plugins doesn't slow anything down or confuse the model — but in practice most people keep two or three active at a time. The rest stay installed and disabled, ready the moment a job calls for them. The mental cost of an active plugin is higher than its runtime cost; keeping the working set small is a human ergonomics choice, not a performance one.

production_viz.label: TWO OR THREE, ACTIVE
production_viz.caption: the rest wait, disabled, not gone

beats.narration_text: One trade-off worth knowing up front: your plugins and everything you taught them live on your machine. Move to a second computer and you set them up again there. The customization is personal — kept local by design, not synced across devices. This works if you value keeping your tuned configuration private; it fails if you rotate machines constantly.

After installing, run one test. Type a slash to see the commands it registered, or just ask it to do the job — build a content calendar for next month, say. A tuned plugin answers noticeably more structured and more aware of your world; an untuned one gives you the domain default. The test tells you which state you're in.
Installing a plugin takes seconds and hands you generic defaults. The conversation afterward — about your actual business, in your actual language — is what makes it yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I just installed a marketing plugin and I want to customize it for my business instead of running the defaults. Interview me the way the customize conversation would — ask what my business does and who my customers are, ask about my voice, my formats, and the terminology I use, then summarize the exact settings you'd apply and show one before-and-after of how a typical output changes once it's tuned to me. Go deeper: which parts of my business would be hardest to encode in a plugin's customization, and what would I lose by not capturing them? Liam, in for Bear.
